# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-11 (Extended v100)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826. **Current narrative point (Autumn Year 3, dual settings)**: (1) Paris, le Petit-Picpus convent district—Valjean and Cosette in sanctuary; M. Gillenormand's residences (Rue Férou, Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire); (2) English provincial harbor towns (Dunstead, Yarlby, Kelford, Staveford, Ravenmere, Ostcombe, Gulhaven, Kelmere, Dunby, Dungate, Torton); Vernon (Colonel Pontmercy's residence). **Environmental conditions (Autumn Year 3)**: children chased hoops down lanes; frost silvered hedges overnight; wind came off water with salt/tar smell; roads rutted and puddled after thaw; light went early; smoke lay flat over fields.

## Primary Locations

**PARIS - LE PETIT-PICPUS DISTRICT**: Between Faubourg Saint-Antoine and la Râpée; Number 62 Rue Petit-Picpus (convent carriage gate). **Convent complex**: Great Convent (Bernardines-Benedictines nuns), Boarding-school, Little Convent (aged nuns). **Interior garden**: Vast oblong with poplar alley, forest trees, gnarled fruit-tree, vegetable beds, melon patch, old well, stone benches. **Chapel**: Window visible from garden. **Burial location**: Mother Crucifixion's vault beneath grand altar. **Vaugirard cemetery**: Ancient burial ground with Prefecture Permission for nightfall interments; former grave-digger Father Mestienne (deceased); replaced by "little Father Lenoir."

**M. GILLENORMAND'S RESIDENCES**: **Rue Férou house** (frequented Madame de T.'s salon twice weekly from 1817 onward)—Madame la Baronne de T., worthy respectable Royalist, salon twice-weekly, tea, royalist politics. **Newly established Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire in the Marais** (after conclusion of Marius's classical studies). Doors closed during day; opens evenings after five o'clock dinner.

**VERNON**: Colonel Pontmercy's residence (smallest house he could find). Reached from Paris by diligence from Rue du Bouloi passing through Vernon at night. **Colonel's grave**: Vaugirard cemetery; black wooden cross with white letters "COLONEL BARON PONTMERCY."

**SAINT-SULPICE CHAPEL**: Location where Marius knelt upon chair inscribed "Monsieur Mabeuf, warden"; Church-warden Mabeuf introduced himself to Marius here.

**QUAI DES ORFÉVRES (Paris)**: Location of engraver where Marius ordered hundred cards bearing name "Le Baron Marius Pontmercy."

**GORBEAU HOVEL (50-52)**: Salpêtrière district, outskirts Paris. Posted "Chambers to let"; inhabited by indigent individuals. **Current tenant—Jondrette family**: Father hired chamber; instructed portress to respond affirmatively if inquired for Pole, Italian, or Spaniard.

**ENGLISH PROVINCIAL SETTINGS**: Dunstead, Yarlby, Kelford, Staveford, Ravenmere, Ostcombe, Gulhaven, Kelmere, Dunby, Dungate, Torton; market towns with parsonages, forges, granaries, ovens, wells, lanes. **Population movements (English locations)**: Yera Haskick left Dunstead for Kelmere; Rinelle quit Kelford for Torton; Kadrek Brackick followed to Torton; Lurald Stenworth told Thizek Stenenridge deed to Kelmere pastures forged; Luena packed trunk, moved Staveford to Dungate; Rozek Stenenridge followed within month; Volan Stenworth (now Peten) mended sleeve by window, said little. **New births (Dunstead)**: Son Ferald Stenworth and daughter Isvie Stenworth born to Luwyn Brackick, father Lurald Stenworth. **Rumor (Dunstead)**: Ismira claimed Wenelle Lindmere drowned crossing estuary (no body seen); Ismira told Luena granary fire was set on purpose (claim/rumor).

## Jean Valjean's Development

**CURRENT STATUS (Autumn Year 3)**: Integrated into convent life as assistant gardener; inhabits old garden hut with Fauchelevent. Works daily; pruner of trees; budded ungrafted orchard trees. **Spiritual transformation**: Meditations on grace; blood ran cold at grateful nuns' songs—realized he justly chastified while wretch shook fist at God. Scaled wall made to escape other expiation now served entrance to sanctuary. Pride vanished; scrutinized heart; wept. All recent months led back to Bishop's holy injunctions—Cosette through love, convent through humility. Knelt in garden walks at eventide; prostrated in prayer. Soul became compounded of silence, perfume, simplicity, joy. Two houses of God received him critically: first when society rejected; second when society pursued.

## Cosette's Development

**INITIAL STATE**: Knew nothing; could say nothing. Unhappiness trained silence. Hardly regained confidence with Valjean. **Convent integration**: Speedily accustomed; regretted Catherine but dared not say. Told Valjean: "Father, if I had known, I would have brought her away." Thinks herself his daughter. Became convent scholar; received pupil garb. Valjean restored mourning suit from Thénardier departure; locked up garments plus stockings/shoes with camphor/aromatics in valise on chair near bed; always carried key. Cosette asked: "Father, what is there in that box which smells so good?" At appointed hour flies to hut filling it with paradise; adored him because sisters melancholy and he kind.

## Fauchelevent's Role

**Identity**: Old crippled gardener admitted approximately two years previously on Valjean's (Mayor Madeleine's) recommendation after cart accident. Limps; takes nearly quarter hour traversing short distances; complains aching back. **Execution of concealment**: Used service door placing Cosette in vintage basket with deaf fruit-seller (Rue Chemin-Vert). Placed Valjean in coffin; transported in hearse to Vaugirard cemetery. Grave-digger Father Mestienne dead; replaced by "little Father Lenoir" (jug red wine). Fauchelevent found lost card, buried corpse, filled grave himself. **Character**: Grateful, talkative, excitable; calls Valjean "Father Madeleine"; peasant of Picardy. Perceived generous action as dying man perceives good wine. Air of convent destroyed personal selfishness; rendered good action absolutely necessary. **Current status**: Lives in garden hut with Valjean; continues gardening; sole person aware of full presence; only known ally/protector. Nuns do not suspect him; eyes fixed on God do not spy.

## Javert's Pursuit

**Reassignment and investigation**: Attached to Paris police after Valjean's escape (January 1823). Newspaper announced Valjean's death (December 1823); Javert remarked "That's a good entry." Police report concerning child abduction in Montfermeil revived memory; suspected Valjean sought daughter. **Secret investigation**: Without telling anyone, took coach to Montfermeil; followed mysterious lodger to Gorbeau house; hired room, listened at lodger's door; Valjean foiled spy by silence. Reasons for secrecy: (1) Indiscretion might alert Valjean; (2) Recapturing ex-convict reputed dead magnificent success; (3) Javert had taste for unforeseen. **Pursuit escalation**: Old woman warned Javert lodger intended to leave; Javert waited behind trees with two men at night. **Escape from Mouffetard**: Valjean cut street lantern rope; Javert found disorder, led astray. Followed from tree to tree; did not arrest hastily. **Current status (Autumn Year 3)**: Established sentinels, organized traps and ambuscades; sure convict could not be far off.

## Marius Pontmercy: Complete Development

**PARENTAGE AND EARLY YEARS**: Son of Colonel Pontmercy (chief of squadron, meagre half-pay); mother Madame Pontmercy (née Gillenormand, youngest daughter—"admirable woman in every sense, lofty in sentiment and rare"). **1815**: Pontmercy married Mademoiselle Gillenormand between two wars; old M. Gillenormand gave consent with sigh. Mother died 1815, leaving child. Colonel's joy in solitude; grandfather imperatively claimed grandson, declaring if child not given would disinherit. Father yielded in child's interest; transferred his love to flowers. Colonel lives alone at Vernon.

**EARLY EDUCATION AND ESTRANGEMENT (Age 7, Spring-Summer Year 3)**: Grandfather kept no relations with son-in-law (colonel "a bandit" to him); colonel called "brigand of the Loire." Never mentioned except with mocking allusions. **Expressly agreed**: Pontmercy never attempt to see or speak to son under penalty of disinheritance. **Secret paternal visits**: Colonel slipped away every two or three months, came to Paris secretly like criminal, posted himself at Saint-Sulpice at hour when Aunt Gillenormand led Marius to mass. Trembling lest aunt turn round, concealed behind pillar, motionless, not daring breathe, gazed at child. Scarred veteran afraid of old spinster. **Correspondence**: Twice yearly (January 1st, St. George's day), Marius wrote duty letters dictated by aunt. Father answered with tender letters grandfather thrust into pocket unread.

**CLASSICAL STUDIES AND TRANSFORMATION**: Conclusion coincided with M. Gillenormand's departure from society. Old man bade farewell to Faubourg Saint-Germain and Madame de T.'s salon; established himself in Marais, Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire. **Summons to Vernon**: Marius seized with trembling fit upon notification to see father. Believed father did not love him (abandoned him to others). Convinced father "the slasher" did not love him. Feeling not beloved, did not love. **Journey to Vernon**: Diligence from Rue du Bouloi took trip to Rouen by night, passed through Vernon. Next day, at twilight, Marius reached Vernon.

**COLONEL'S DEATH AND AFTERMATH**: Colonel attacked by brain fever three days previously. Written to M. Gillenormand demanding son. Malady grown worse. On very evening of Marius's arrival at Vernon, colonel had attack of delirium; rose from bed crying: "My son is not coming! I shall go to meet him!" Ran out of room, fell prostrate on floor of antechamber. Had just expired. **Marius's first sight of father**: Gazed upon man he beheld for first time—venerable and manly face, open eyes which saw not, white locks, robust limbs marked by sword-thrusts (brown lines) and bullet-holes (red stars). Contemplated gigantic scar stamping heroism on countenance on which God had imprinted goodness. Felt ashamed and embarrassed at his own attitude; held hat in hand; dropped it on floor to produce impression grief had deprived him of strength to hold it. Was stranger there among grieving servants and priest.

**PATERNAL LEGACY AND DOCUMENT**: Colonel left written instruction: "_For my son_.—The Emperor made me a Baron on the battle-field of Waterloo. Since the Restoration disputes my right to this title which I purchased with my blood, my son shall take it and bear it. That he will be worthy of it is a matter of course." Below, the colonel had added: "At that same battle of Waterloo, a sergeant saved my life. The man's name was Thénardier. I think that he has recently been keeping a little inn, in a village in the neighborhood of Paris, at Chelles or Montfermeil. If my son meets him, he will do all the good he can to Thénardier."

**INTELLECTUAL AND POLITICAL TRANSFORMATION**: Preserved religious habits of childhood. One Sunday went to hear mass at Saint-Sulpice. Knelt upon chair inscribed "Monsieur Mabeuf, warden." Church-warden Mabeuf presented himself and spoke to Marius, told him about life at Vernon, colonel's retreat, his flowers, his solitude. Marius came to full knowledge of that rare, sweet, and sublime man, that species of lion-lamb which was his father.

**READING AND NAPOLEON CONVERSION**: Read _Moniteur_, all histories of Republic and Empire, _Memorial de Sainte-Hélène_, all memoirs, newspapers, bulletins, proclamations; devoured everything. First time encountered father's name in bulletins of grand army, had fever for week. Went to see generals under whom Georges Pontmercy served. Church-warden Mabeuf, whom he visited again, encouraged this study. **From infancy imbued with party of 1814 judgments on Bonaparte**: Prejudices of Restoration tended to disfigure Napoleon. Execrated him even more than Robespierre. Party of 1814 cleverly turned to account nation's fatigue and hatred of mothers. Bonaparte became almost fabulous monster. Marius had never entertained about "_that man_" any other ideas; combined with tenacity in his nature.

**REVELATION THROUGH STUDY**: On reading history, studying documents and materials, veil concealing Napoleon gradually rent. Caught glimpse of something immense; suspected he had been deceived about Bonaparte as about all rest. Each day saw more distinctly; set about mounting slowly, step by step, almost regretfully at beginning, then with intoxication and as though attracted by irresistible fascination. One night alone in little chamber near roof, reading bulletins of grand army, beheld his father's name interspersed with Emperor's name; felt flood swelling and rising within him; thought he heard drums, cannon, trumpets, measured tread of battalions, dull distant gallop of cavalry; eyes raised heavenward gazed upon colossal constellations gleaming in measureless depths of space, then fell upon book; heart contracted; in transport, trembling, panting. All at once, without knowing what impelled him, sprang to feet, stretched both arms out of window, gazed intently into gloom, silence, infinite darkness, eternal immensity, and exclaimed: "Long live the Emperor!"

**METAMORPHOSIS**: From that moment, all was over. The Ogre of Corsica, usurper, tyrant, monster, actor, poisoner, tiger, Buonaparte—all vanished, gave place to vague brilliant radiance in which shone, at inaccessible height, pale marble phantom of Cæsar. Emperor for his father only well-beloved captain whom one admires; for Marius became something more. Predestined constructor of French group, succeeding Roman group in domination of universe. **New conviction intoxicated him; hurled himself headlong into adhesion; went too far**. Nature so constructed; once on downward slope, almost impossible to put on brake. Fanaticism for sword took possession; complicated enthusiasm for idea. Did not perceive that along with genius, pell-mell, admitted force—installing in two compartments of idolatry: on one hand divine, on other brutal. **Violent sort of good faith which took everything in lump**.

**ORDERED CARDS**: When entirely shed old Bourbon and ultra skin, became thoroughly revolutionist, profoundly democratic and republican, went to engraver on Quai des Orfévres and ordered hundred cards bearing name: _Le Baron Marius Pontmercy_.

**ESTRANGEMENT FROM GRANDFATHER**: By natural consequence, receded from grandfather in proportion as drew nearer to father and colonel's memory. M. Gillenormand's temper did not please him. All dissonances of grave young man and frivolous old man existed between them. **Nothing betrayed on exterior**: Only grew colder and colder; laconic at meals, rare in house. When aunt scolded, very gentle, alleged studies, lectures, examinations as pretext. **Grandfather's diagnosis**: "In love! I know all about it."

**QUEST FOR THÉNARDIER**: On one of brief trips, went to Montfermeil to obey injunction father left—sought old sergeant to Waterloo, inn-keeper Thénardier. Thénardier had failed, inn closed, no one knew what became of him. Marius away from house four days on this quest.

**RECENT CONFRONTATION (Autumn Year 3)**: Marius returned from Vernon third day, descended at grandfather's door. M. Gillenormand had heard his entrance, climbed stairs to embrace him and question him. Marius had thrown off travelling-coat and black ribbon worn round neck. M. Gillenormand held one of Marius's cards (bearing name "Le Baron Marius Pontmercy") in his hand. Upon seeing Marius, grandfather exclaimed with air of bourgeois and grinning superiority.

**VIOLENT QUARREL (Autumn Year 3)**: Marius retorted with downcast eyes and severe air: "My father was a humble and heroic man, who served the Republic and France gloriously, who was great in the greatest history that men have ever made, who lived in the bivouac for a quarter of a century, beneath grape-shot and bullets, in snow and mud by day, beneath rain at night, who captured two flags, who received twenty wounds, who died forgotten and abandoned, and who never committed but one mistake, which was to love too fondly two ingrates, his country and myself."

M. Gillenormand rose and sprang to feet. Every word produced effect of puffs of air from forge upon blazing brand. From dull hue turned red, from red purple, from purple flame-colored. Cried: "Marius! Abominable child! I do not know what your father was! I do not wish to know! But what I do know is, that there never was anything but scoundrels among those men! They were all rascals, assassins, red-caps, thieves! I say all! I say all! I know not one! I say all! You are no more a baron than my slipper is! They were all bandits in the service of Robespierre! All who served B-u-o-naparté were brigands! They were all traitors who betrayed their legitimate king! All cowards who fled before the Prussians and the English at Waterloo! That is what I do know!"

**MARIUS'S ANGUISH**: Marius quivered in every limb, did not know what would happen next, brain on fire. Like priest beholding sacred wafers cast to winds, fakir beholding passer-by spit upon idol. Impossible for him to insult grandfather yet equally impossible for him to leave father unavenged. On one hand sacred grave, on other hoary locks.

**OLD MAN'S RESPONSE**: Who had been crimson, turned whiter than his hair. Wheeled round towards bust of M. le Duc de Berry on chimney-piece, made profound bow with peculiar majesty. Then paced twice, slowly and in silence, from fireplace to window and from window to fireplace, traversing whole length of room, making polished floor creak as though stone statue walking.

**MARIUS'S DEPARTURE IN INDIGNATION**: Went forth in indignation. **Lost paternal document (critical loss)**: While carrying Marius's "duds" precipitately to his chamber at grandfather's command, Nicolette had inadvertently let fall, probably on attic staircase, that medallion of black shagreen which contained paper penned by colonel. Neither paper nor case could afterwards be found. Marius convinced that "Monsieur Gillenormand"—from that day forth he never alluded to him otherwise—had flung "his father's testament" in fire. He knew by heart few lines which colonel had written, and consequently nothing was lost. But paper, writing, that sacred relic,—all that was his very heart.

## M. Gillenormand and His World

**IDENTITY AND CHARACTER**: Worthy bourgeois; "consideration of absolutely first-rate quality"; dignified, honest, lofty in bourgeois fashion; great age added venerable dishevelment. **Witticisms**: When King of Prussia visited as "Count de Ruppin," approved: "All kings who are not King of France are provincial kings." **TWO DAUGHTERS**: Born ten years apart. **Youngest** (Marius's mother): Charming soul turned towards light, occupied with flowers, verses, music; ethereal; wedded to vague heroic figure; died 1815. **Eldest** (Mademoiselle Gillenormand): Over forty, looked fifty; antique virtue, incombustible prude. Outside family, no one knew first name. Revered "holy blood," venerated "sacred heart." Household of old man and old spinster touching aspect of two weaknesses leaning for support. **Servants**: Chambermaid Nicolette (succeeded to Magnon); short-breathed pursy Basque; porter.

**LIEUTENANT THÉODULE GILLENORMAND**: Great-grand-nephew on paternal side; led garrison life, outside family and far from domestic hearth. Lieutenant fulfilled conditions required to make "fine officer." Had "lady's waist," victorious manner of trailing sword and twirling moustache in hook. Visited Paris very rarely; Marius had never seen him. Cousins knew each other only by name. **Favorite of Aunt Gillenormand** because she did not see him; not seeing people permits attributing all possible perfections. **Recent visit (Autumn Year 3)**: Théodule entered aunt's chamber while she worked on embroidery of Empire and Restoration (with numerous cart-wheels) to distract herself from curiosity about Marius's absences. She uttered cry of delight at seeing lancer enter her chamber.

**THÉODULE'S DISCOVERY AT VERNON**: While at Vernon (details of his presence unclear), Théodule encountered Marius kneeling in cemetery upon grave. Marius had strewn bouquet there. At extremity of grave, on little swelling marking head, stood cross of black wood with name in white letters: COLONEL BARON PONTMERCY. Marius's sobs were audible. Théodule absolutely put out of countenance by unexpected encounter with sepulchre; experienced singular and disagreeable sensation composed of respect for tomb mingled with respect for colonel. Retreated, leaving Marius alone in cemetery; there was discipline in retreat. Death appeared to him with large epaulets, and he almost made military salute to it. **Not knowing what to write to aunt about this discovery of Marius's love affairs, Théodule decided not to write at all**; it is probable that nothing would have resulted from his discovery if scene at Vernon had not had almost immediate counter-shock at Paris.
